title: ZBiotics vs Morning Recovery: Which Hangover Drink Is Worth It?
excerpt: ZBiotics vs Morning Recovery, compared honestly: how the probiotic drink and the DHM drink work, when to take each, cost per night, and what the evidence shows.
metaDescription: ZBiotics vs Morning Recovery: how the probiotic and the DHM drink work, when to take each, cost per night, safety, and which one is worth trying.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** ZBiotics and Morning Recovery are both drinks you take around a night out, but they work in completely different ways and you take them at different times. ZBiotics is a probiotic drink made with a bacterium engineered to break down acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol) in your gut, and you drink it *before* your first drink. Morning Recovery, from More Labs, is a small bottle of DHM (dihydromyricetin, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol in the body and brain) plus electrolytes, vitamins, and milk thistle, and you drink it *during or after* drinking, usually before bed. Neither has a published, independent clinical trial showing that the finished product reduces hangovers.

**The quick verdict:** If you'd rather have something rooted in a larger body of published research, and you want it cheaper per night, Morning Recovery is the more sensible pick of the two. If you're curious about the gut-acetaldehyde idea and don't mind paying well over ten dollars a night, ZBiotics is a reasonable experiment. If what you actually want is DHM, plain DHM capsules give you more of it for much less money than either bottle. And nothing in any bottle replaces eating, drinking water, and drinking less.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares two consumer products using published research and the companies' own descriptions. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Neither product is approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, neither lowers your blood alcohol, and neither makes it safe to drive. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if** you take prescription medicine (especially sedatives, sleep aids, anti-seizure drugs, blood thinners, or anything processed heavily by the liver), are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, or have a weakened immune system. **Call 911 if** someone who has been drinking is confused, vomiting while drowsy, breathing slowly or irregularly, has pale or bluish skin, or can't be woken up. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no hangover product helps with that.

We don't have an affiliate relationship with ZBiotics or More Labs, so there are no links to buy either product on this page. We do earn a commission on some DHM products mentioned near the end, and we say so where they appear.

## ZBiotics vs Morning Recovery at a Glance

| | ZBiotics Pre-Alcohol Probiotic | Morning Recovery (More Labs) |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Small single-serve drink | Small single-serve drink |
| Main active ingredient | *Bacillus subtilis* probiotic engineered to break down acetaldehyde | DHM from *Hovenia dulcis* extract, plus electrolytes, vitamins, and milk thistle |
| What it targets | Acetaldehyde made in the gut | Alcohol's effects on the brain and liver (DHM), plus fluids and minerals |
| When you take it | Before your first drink | During or after drinking, ideally before sleep |
| Typical cost per night | Roughly $10 to $15 | Several dollars a bottle in multipacks |
| Published trial of the finished product | None independent that we could find | None that we could find |
| Research behind the main ingredient | Mostly company research | DHM: university lab and animal research, limited human data |
| Genetically engineered | Yes | No |

Prices change often and depend on pack size, retailer, and subscriptions, so treat those figures as a rough guide and check current pricing yourself. Formulas change too. Read the label on the bottle in front of you.

## The Core Difference: When and Where Each One Works

Most comparisons of hangover products line up ingredients. With these two, the more useful thing to understand is timing, because it follows directly from how each one is supposed to work.

When you drink, your body breaks down alcohol in two steps. First, an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into **acetaldehyde**, which is toxic. Then a second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is much less harmful. Most of this happens in your liver, but some of it also happens in your digestive tract, partly through the bacteria that already live there.

- **ZBiotics** tries to help with the second step, but only in your gut. Its bacteria need to be in your intestines while alcohol is passing through, so the company tells you to drink it before you start. Taking it the next morning doesn't fit the mechanism at all.
- **Morning Recovery** relies mainly on DHM, which researchers think works on the body as a whole, after alcohol has been absorbed. Animal research suggests DHM may affect how the brain responds to alcohol and may support the liver enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde. Because of that, it's taken while you're drinking or before bed, when alcohol is still in your system. Despite the name, it isn't meant to be a morning-after drink.

So these aren't really substitutes for the same job. One is a pre-game gut product. The other is an end-of-night whole-body product with some hydration thrown in.

## How ZBiotics Works

ZBiotics calls its product a "pre-alcohol probiotic." The active ingredient is a strain of *Bacillus subtilis*, a bacterium with a long history in food. It's the organism used to ferment natto, a traditional Japanese soybean dish, and other strains are sold as ordinary probiotics. The ZBiotics strain has been genetically engineered to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde. Because *B. subtilis* forms tough spores, the company says the bacteria survive the stomach and become active in the intestines.

The idea is clever and the biotechnology is real. There's no reason to doubt that the strain makes the enzyme and can break down acetaldehyde in a lab.

### The honest limits of the ZBiotics idea

There are two big open questions, and they're not small ones.

1. **Location.** Bacteria in your gut can only reach acetaldehyde in your gut. Most acetaldehyde is made in your liver, and ZBiotics can't touch that. Even if it works exactly as designed, it can only affect a slice of your total acetaldehyde exposure, and how big that slice is hasn't been well established.
2. **Whether acetaldehyde is the main cause of hangovers.** Hangover researchers generally describe the hangover as having several overlapping causes: an inflammatory immune response, poor sleep, fluid and hormone changes, low blood sugar in some people, and by-products in certain drinks. Acetaldehyde may play a part, but by the time symptoms peak the next morning, much of it has usually been cleared. A product that targets acetaldehyde alone may only touch part of the picture.

On the evidence side, we haven't found an independent, peer-reviewed, randomized trial showing that ZBiotics reduces hangover symptoms in people. The company points to its own research. That isn't worthless, but it isn't the same as an independent trial with the full data published for others to check. Our [full ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) goes through the science, the Reddit sentiment, and the GMO question in more detail.

## How Morning Recovery Works

Morning Recovery is a few-ounce bottle made by More Labs, a Los Angeles company. It launched in the late 2010s after a crowdfunding campaign and was one of the first widely marketed drinks in the US built around DHM. The brand has sold several versions, including an original formula with sugar and a zero-sugar version.

The main ingredients on its labels have generally fallen into four groups:

1. **Hovenia dulcis extract,** the Oriental raisin tree, which is the DHM source and the headline ingredient.
2. **Milk thistle,** a herbal supplement marketed for liver support. There isn't good evidence that it prevents hangovers.
3. **Electrolytes,** such as potassium. Sensible after drinking, though the amounts in a small bottle are modest next to a proper rehydration drink.
4. **Vitamins,** mainly B vitamins and sometimes vitamin C. There's little evidence that a single dose of vitamins changes how you feel the next morning.

### The honest limits of the Morning Recovery idea

The biggest issue is **dose**. Several versions of Morning Recovery have listed DHM as part of an extract or blend rather than giving a clear number of milligrams of pure DHM. "Hovenia dulcis extract" isn't the same as pure DHM, so you often can't tell exactly how much DHM you're getting. Independent reviewers have generally estimated that a bottle delivers a few hundred milligrams at most, which is at the low end next to the 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving found in many single-ingredient DHM products.

The second issue is the evidence. We're not aware of any published, placebo-controlled trial of Morning Recovery itself. Its scientific case is borrowed from DHM research in general. That research is more substantial than what exists for the ZBiotics approach, but it's still mostly animal and lab work. The best-known paper is a 2012 study in rats by Shen and colleagues from Jing Liang's lab at UCLA, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, which found that DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal-like effects in rats. Human hangover data remain limited. Our [Morning Recovery review](/never-hungover/more-labs-morning-recovery-review) covers the ingredients, the lab heritage, and the value math in full.

## Morning Recovery vs ZBiotics: Which Has Better Evidence?

People search this both ways round, "ZBiotics vs Morning Recovery" and "Morning Recovery vs ZBiotics," and the answer doesn't change with the order. Here's the plain comparison.

**For the finished products,** it's roughly a tie, and not in a good way. Neither has an independent, published, randomized trial in people showing it reduces hangovers.

**For the main ingredient,** Morning Recovery has the edge. DHM has been studied by several research groups, in animals and in the lab, with a small amount of human work. The ZBiotics mechanism rests mainly on the company's own research and on general knowledge of *B. subtilis*. More published research doesn't mean DHM is proven in people, but it does mean more independent scientists have looked at it.

**For the plausibility of the mechanism,** both have a real weakness. ZBiotics can only reach gut acetaldehyde. Morning Recovery may simply not contain enough DHM to matter, and you often can't tell from the label.

It's also worth keeping the whole category in perspective. A widely cited systematic review of randomized trials, published in the *BMJ* in 2005, found no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary remedy reliably prevents or treats hangovers. Some small studies since then have been encouraging for particular ingredients, such as a small 2020 trial of L-cysteine published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism*, but none of this has turned any product into a dependable fix. A 2019 crossover trial published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* also found that the order you drink in ("beer before liquor") made no difference to hangovers, while how much people drank mattered far more. That's the theme running through all hangover research: the amount you drink is the biggest lever you have.

## Timing: How to Take Each One

Getting the timing wrong is the most common way people end up thinking a product "didn't work."

**ZBiotics:**
- Drink one bottle before your first alcoholic drink, following the label.
- Don't take it the next morning. By then, the alcohol has already passed through your gut.
- The company recommends one serving for a typical night. Check the label for its current guidance on longer nights.

**Morning Recovery:**
- Drink one bottle during your night out or after your last drink, ideally before sleep.
- Taking it at noon the next day gives the DHM much less to work with, because most of the alcohol is gone by then.
- Drinking a glass of water with it is a good idea. One small bottle doesn't replace the fluid you lose from drinking.

If you're the kind of person who forgets things at the start of the night, Morning Recovery's timing is more forgiving. If you're the kind of person who forgets things at the end of the night, ZBiotics' timing suits you better. That sounds trivial, but a product only helps if you actually take it at the right time.

## Price per Night Out: Both Cost More Than the Ingredients Suggest

Price is where the gap between these two is clearest.

**ZBiotics** usually costs roughly $10 to $15 a bottle, sometimes less with subscriptions or bulk packs. If you go out once or twice a week, that's hundreds of dollars a year.

**Morning Recovery** has generally cost several dollars a bottle in multipacks. That's noticeably cheaper per night than ZBiotics, but still expensive for the amount of DHM you're likely getting.

**Plain DHM capsules** are much cheaper. For example, a single-ingredient DHM product can cost under a dollar per serving and list 1,000 mg of DHM on the label, which is more DHM than most estimates for a bottle of Morning Recovery.

A fair way to compare DHM products is cost per milligram of DHM, not cost per serving:

1. Find the price of one serving.
2. Find the DHM in that serving. If the label only gives an extract or blend amount, you can't do the math, and that's useful information in itself.
3. Divide the price by the milligrams of DHM.

ZBiotics doesn't fit this math because it doesn't contain DHM. The question there is simply whether the experiment is worth $10 to $15 to you, given the evidence.

What you pay extra for with both drinks is convenience: a ready-to-go bottle, a flavor some people like, and an easy routine. That's a legitimate thing to pay for. Just choose it on purpose rather than assuming a higher price means a stronger product.

## Can You Take ZBiotics and Morning Recovery Together?

There's no known interaction between a *B. subtilis* probiotic and DHM, and because they act at different times and in different places, nothing in how they work suggests they'd clash. Some people do stack a pre-drinking product with an end-of-night one.

That said, there's no evidence that combining them works better than either one alone, and you'd be paying for both, which pushes a single night well past $15. If you want to test whether either one helps you, it's more informative to try one at a time on similar nights. Stacking two products, plus water, plus food, makes it impossible to tell what made the difference.

The one combination to take seriously is with your own medicines. DHM is a plant compound that's processed by the liver, and its effect on how other drugs are processed hasn't been studied much in people. If you take prescription medicine, check with a pharmacist before adding any DHM product. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what's known and what isn't.

## Side Effects and Safety: Who Should Be Careful With Each

For most healthy adults, both products appear to be low-risk at label doses. The differences are about who should check first.

**ZBiotics:**
- May cause mild bloating, gas, or bowel changes in some people, like other probiotics.
- People with weakened immune systems (for example during chemotherapy or after an organ transplant) should talk to a doctor before using any live-bacteria product. Rare infections from probiotic organisms have been reported in very ill patients.
- Antibiotics can kill the bacteria and make it less likely to do anything.
- If you prefer to avoid genetically engineered foods, that's a valid reason to skip it, though the engineering itself isn't evidence of harm.

**Morning Recovery:**
- Some people report mild stomach upset or a taste they don't enjoy. The original formula contains sugar, which matters if you're watching sugar intake. The zero-sugar version uses non-sugar sweeteners.
- DHM's long-term safety in people hasn't been studied in large trials. Short-term use at common doses hasn't raised obvious red flags in the available research.
- People with liver or kidney disease, people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and anyone on prescription medication should check with a doctor first.

**For both:** any stomach upset the night of or the morning after is far more likely to come from the alcohol than from either product. The bigger safety risk isn't the bottle, it's the false sense of security. If a hangover product leads you to drink more than you would have, or to drive because you "feel fine," it has made things worse. Neither product lowers your blood alcohol.

### When to see a doctor after drinking

Most hangovers are miserable but pass within a day. Get medical help if you notice any of these:

- **Right away (call 911):** confusion, vomiting while drowsy or unable to stay awake, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, pale or bluish skin, or someone who can't be woken up. These point to alcohol poisoning.
- **Soon:** vomiting that won't stop or that contains blood, being unable to keep fluids down for many hours, chest pain, a racing or pounding heart that doesn't settle, or yellow skin or eyes.
- **If it's becoming a pattern:** shaking, sweating, or anxiety that shows up when you go without a drink, or needing a drink in the morning to feel normal. That's more than a hangover, and it's worth a plain conversation with a doctor, who can help you stop or cut back safely.

## Pros and Cons

### ZBiotics

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Novel, real mechanism (engineered acetaldehyde-degrading bacteria) | No independent, peer-reviewed human trial on hangovers that we could find |
| Based on a common, food-safe bacterium | Can only act on gut acetaldehyde, not acetaldehyde made in the liver |
| Simple routine: one bottle before you start | Acetaldehyde isn't established as the main cause of hangovers |
| Generally well tolerated | Expensive, often $10 to $15 a night |
| No DHM, so an option for people avoiding plant extracts | Useless if you forget it at the start of the night |

### Morning Recovery

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Built around DHM, which has more published research than most hangover ingredients | No published trial of the finished product |
| Convenient, ready-to-drink bottle | DHM dose is often unclear from the label and likely modest |
| Adds some electrolytes and fluid | Electrolyte amounts are small next to a real rehydration drink |
| Cheaper per night than ZBiotics | Much more expensive per milligram of DHM than plain capsules |
| Forgiving timing (during or after drinking) | Original formula contains sugar |

## Who Should Pick Which

**ZBiotics may suit you if:**
- You're curious about the engineered-probiotic approach and the cost doesn't bother you.
- You reliably remember to take things before you go out.
- You want something that doesn't contain DHM or herbal extracts.

**Morning Recovery may suit you if:**
- You want a DHM-based product but prefer a drink to a pill.
- You tend to remember a product at the end of the night rather than the start.
- You like the idea of getting a little extra fluid and some electrolytes at the same time.

**Neither may be the best fit if:**
- Price matters. Plain DHM capsules plus a glass of water or a cheap electrolyte packet cover the same ground as Morning Recovery for much less, and with a clearly labeled dose.
- You're hoping a product will let you drink a lot without consequences. No product does that.

## The Verdict

Between these two, Morning Recovery is the more practical choice for most people. Its main ingredient has more independent research behind it, its timing is more forgiving, and it costs less per night. ZBiotics is the more interesting idea scientifically, but it rests mostly on company research, it can only reach a fraction of the acetaldehyde your body makes, and it's the most expensive option per night in this category.

The honest caveat is that neither product has strong independent human evidence, so "better" here means "more reasonable to try," not "proven to work." If you try either one, try it on a few similar nights, keep everything else the same, and judge it on whether you'd pay for it again. Our [DHM vs ZBiotics comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics) and [ZBiotics vs Cheers comparison](/never-hungover/zbiotics-vs-cheers) cover the other matchups people most often weigh, and our guide to [hangover probiotics](/never-hungover/hangover-probiotics) looks at the probiotic idea more broadly.

## The Basics That Matter More Than Either Bottle

Whatever you choose, these habits do more for the next morning than any product in this category:

- **Drink less, or drink slower.** The amount of alcohol is the single biggest factor in how bad a hangover is. Pacing at about one drink an hour gives your body a better chance to keep up.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks helps with fluid loss and naturally slows you down. Our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains when extra minerals actually help.
- **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, and poor sleep makes everything feel worse. Stopping a couple of hours before bed helps.
- **Have a plan for getting home** that doesn't involve driving.

Our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each of these in more detail.

## The DHM Option: More DHM Than Morning Recovery, for Less

If this comparison points you toward DHM, a plain DHM supplement is the simplest way to get it with a clearly labeled dose. These are affiliate links, which means we may earn a commission if you buy, at no extra cost to you.

- [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is our value pick: 1,000 mg of DHM per serving at about $0.80 per serving at the price we last tracked. Pair it with a glass of water and you've covered the main parts of a Morning Recovery bottle for a fraction of the cost.
- [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is our top-rated pick if you want an all-in-one formula. It pairs 1,000 mg of DHM with L-cysteine, milk thistle, and electrolytes, at about $1.93 per serving at the price we last tracked.

Like any DHM product, these are taken around drinking or before bed, not the next afternoon. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [full DHM reviews](/reviews) compare the major brands on dose, purity, and price. There is no good evidence that any DHM product, including these, can make a heavy night consequence-free. They're aimed at making a reasonable night a bit easier.

## The Bottom Line

- **ZBiotics** is an engineered probiotic you drink before your first drink. It targets acetaldehyde in the gut only, rests mostly on company research, and costs roughly $10 to $15 a night.
- **Morning Recovery** is a DHM-based drink with electrolytes and vitamins that you take during or after drinking. DHM has more published research (mostly in animals), but the dose per bottle is often unclear and likely modest.
- **Neither finished product** has an independent published trial showing it reduces hangovers.
- **Morning Recovery is the more practical pick** of the two for most people. Plain DHM capsules plus water beat both on value.
- **No product replaces** eating, pacing, water, and drinking less, and none makes driving after drinking safe.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is ZBiotics or Morning Recovery better for hangovers?**

Neither has an independent published trial showing it reduces hangovers, so there's no proven winner. Morning Recovery is the more practical pick for most people: its main ingredient, DHM, has more published research (mostly in animals), its timing is more forgiving, and it costs less per night. ZBiotics is an interesting idea but rests mostly on company research and costs roughly $10 to $15 a night.

**Morning Recovery vs ZBiotics: what's the main difference?**

They work in different places and at different times. ZBiotics is a probiotic you drink before your first drink, and its engineered bacteria break down acetaldehyde in your gut. Morning Recovery is a DHM drink with electrolytes and vitamins that you take during or after drinking, usually before bed. DHM is thought to act on the brain and liver after alcohol has been absorbed.

**When should I take ZBiotics vs Morning Recovery?**

Take ZBiotics before your first alcoholic drink, because the bacteria need to be in your gut while alcohol passes through. Take Morning Recovery during your night out or after your last drink, ideally before sleep. Despite its name, Morning Recovery isn't meant to be taken the next morning, and ZBiotics doesn't work as a morning-after drink either.

**Can you take ZBiotics and Morning Recovery together?**

There's no known interaction between them, and they act at different times, so combining them isn't expected to cause problems for healthy adults. But there's no evidence that the combination works better than either one alone, and it makes a single night expensive. If you take prescription medicine, ask a pharmacist before using any DHM product.

**Does Morning Recovery have DHM?**

Yes. Morning Recovery uses Hovenia dulcis extract, a natural source of DHM, as its headline ingredient. Several versions have listed it as an extract or part of a blend rather than as a clear milligram amount of pure DHM, so the exact dose is often hard to tell. Independent estimates generally put it at a few hundred milligrams at most.

**Does ZBiotics contain DHM?**

No. ZBiotics contains a genetically engineered strain of Bacillus subtilis, a common food bacterium, designed to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde. It doesn't contain DHM. That's why some people pair a probiotic approach with a DHM product, though there's no evidence the combination works better.

**Which is cheaper, ZBiotics or Morning Recovery?**

Morning Recovery is usually cheaper per night, generally several dollars a bottle in multipacks, while ZBiotics often costs roughly $10 to $15 a bottle. Plain DHM capsules are cheaper than both, often under a dollar per serving with a clearly labeled DHM dose. Prices change, so check current pricing before you buy.

**Do ZBiotics or Morning Recovery lower blood alcohol?**

No. Neither product lowers your blood alcohol level, sobers you up faster, or makes it safe to drive. ZBiotics targets acetaldehyde, not alcohol, and the company says so itself. DHM has shown effects on intoxication in rats, but there is no good evidence that it lowers blood alcohol in people.
